title: Platform Systems & Services — Runbooks, Dashboards, Alerts, and Roadmap (Q2 2028)
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Purpose

This page consolidates the Platform Systems & Services operating runbooks, dashboard definitions and alert thresholds, common how-tos for oncall and engineers, a short retrospective from the last quarter, and the roadmap for Q2 2028. It is the canonical team wiki for day-to-day platform operations and mid-term planning.

Table of contents
1. Overview
2. Runbooks (critical services)
3. Dashboards & Alerting
4. How-tos — common procedures
5. Retrospective (Q1 2028)
6. Roadmap (Q2 2028)
7. Team wiki / operational contacts
8. Appendix & links

1) Overview
The Platform Systems & Services team owns the runtime and orchestration layer for Redwood’s hosted and dedicated deployments: API gateway, request routers, autoscaling controllers, cache layers, and metrics/observability. This document covers operational guidance for the services listed below and the dashboards/alerts we use to detect regressions against our SLOs.

Primary production services referenced in this document:
- api-router (service name: platform-api-router) — external ingress for Redwood API requests
- inference-queue (service name: inference-queue) — request broker between front-end and worker pool
- runtime-pool-manager (service name: runtime-pool) — autoscaling + allocation of GPU capacity
- kv-cache (service name: platform-kvcache) — in-memory prefix / KV cache for model sessions
- metrics-collector (service name: platform-metrics) — central metric ingestion pipeline

Service owners (high-level)
- api-router: Owning oncall - @miguel (Miguel Alvarez); primary team - eng-platform
- runtime-pool: Owning oncall - @lena (Lena Chang); primary team - eng-platform
- inference-queue: Owning oncall - @priya (Priya Nair); primary team - eng-serving-runtime
- kv-cache: Owning oncall - @sam (Samir Gupta); primary team - eng-infra
- metrics-collector: Owning oncall - @olivia (Olivia Reed); primary team - eng-sre

2) Runbooks (critical services)
Each runbook below follows a simple template: Symptoms, Impact, Immediate mitigation (1-3 steps), Recovery steps, Postmortem owner.

2.a) api-router — 502/504 flood or increased p50/p99 latency
Symptoms:
1) Sharp increase in 5xx responses (502/504) reported in platform-api-router dashboard
2) Elevated request queue length in api-router > 2000
Impact: External latency increase; user-facing errors; can trigger downstream autoscaling thrash.
Immediate mitigation:
1) Toggle rate-limiter to 50% by running: 
   kubectl -n platform exec deploy/api-router -- curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/__admin/rate_limit -d '{"factor":0.5}'
2) Route a 10% sample of traffic to standby region (eu-west-1) using traffic-router config: 
   ./cli traffic-router set-split --service api-router --split '{"us-east-1":0.9, "eu-west-1":0.1}'
Recovery steps:
1) Identify upstream causes (spikes from a customer, backend timeouts). Check inference-queue backlog and runtime-pool activity.
2) Roll back recent config changes (deploy tags) in the last 15 minutes: 
   git log --since='15 minutes' --pretty=oneline -- path=deploy/api-router
3) If error rates persist, increase pod count by 30% with controlled rollout: 
   kubectl scale deployment api-router --replicas=<current*1.3> --namespace platform
Postmortem owner: Miguel Alvarez

2.b) runtime-pool — insufficient GPU capacity / scheduling failures
Symptoms:
- Pending pods in runtime-pool > 50 for > 10m
- Scheduler errors: "no matching instance" in cluster-events
Impact: Increased latency and token cost due to fallback to smaller model variants; potential request failures.
Immediate mitigation:
1) Enable burst-capacity policy: 
   curl -X POST "https://control-plane.internal/v1/pools/runtime-pool/burst" -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' -d '{"duration_sec":900}'
2) Temporarily shift low-priority traffic to warm-only pool: 
   ./poolctl set-priority --pool=runtime-pool --min-alloc=0.15
Recovery steps:
1) Inspect autoscaler logs: kubectl logs deploy/autoscaler -n platform | grep scale
2) If autoscaler is healthy but capacity insufficient, request capacity increase via cloud portal (ticket template in Appendix).
Postmortem owner: Lena Chang

2.c) kv-cache — cache thrash or high eviction rates
Symptoms:
- Eviction rate > 5% sustained for 30m
- Cache hit ratio drops below 70%
Impact: Increased backend model token compute and latency; higher cost per request.
Immediate mitigation:
1) Increase cache TTL for session-prefixed keys: 
   redis-cli -h kv-cache.cluster config set volatile-ttl 120000
2) If memory pressure high, enable read-through fallback: 
   kubectl patch deploy/kv-proxy -n platform --patch '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"annotations":{"kv-readthrough":"enabled"}}}}}'
Recovery steps:
1) Run cache heatmap to identify hot prefixes: 
   ./tools/cache-heatmap --days=1 --top=100
2) Work with product to add targeted session-level caching for heavy customers.
Postmortem owner: Samir Gupta

3) Dashboards & Alerting
Goals and SLOs
- API Availability SLO: 99.95% successful 2xx/3xx responses for platform-api-router (measured monthly)
- Request latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) for platform-api-router: p50 < 60ms, p95 < 200ms, p99 < 500ms (global)
- Mean time to mitigate (MTTM) target for P1 incidents: < 20 minutes

Key dashboards (names in Grafana)
- platform/api-router/overview — latency, errors, request rate, upstream response codes, queue length
- platform/runtime-pool/health — capacity, pending pods, instance failures, scale events
- platform/kv-cache/overview — hit ratio, eviction rate, memory usage, top prefixes
- platform/ingress-security — TLS errors, blocked requests, client auth failures
- platform/metrics-ingest — metric lag, dropped samples, kafka lag (if present)

Alerting table (thresholds are tuned for Q2 2028)
| Alert name | Trigger | Severity | Runbook | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| api-router-high-5xx | > 1% 5xx over 5m (rate-adjusted) | P1 | api-router | @miguel |
| api-router-latency-p99 | p99 > 800ms for 10m | P1 | api-router | @miguel |
| runtime-pool-pending | pending pods > 30 for 10m | P1 | runtime-pool | @lena |
| kvcache-eviction-high | eviction-rate > 5% for 30m | P2 | kv-cache | @sam |
| metrics-lagging | ingestion lag > 120s | P2 | metrics-collector | @olivia |

Alerting playbook highlights:
- All P1 alerts page to #platform-oncall Slack channel and immediately page the oncall via PagerDuty. Escalation policy: 0–10m to oncall, 10–20m escalate to platform lead, >20m invoke incident bridge.
- Use alert annotations to link directly to runbook sections. Each alert must include: detection query, runbook link, last deploy timestamp.

4) How-tos — common procedures
A) How to collect a heap profile from runtime-pool container
1) Identify pod: kubectl -n platform get pods -l app=runtime-worker
2) Exec and run heap capture: kubectl -n platform exec -it <pod> -- /usr/local/bin/heapdump --output /tmp/heap-$(date +%s).prof
3) Copy to analysis host: kubectl -n platform cp <pod>:/tmp/heap-*.prof ./
4) Upload to symbol store: ./tools/upload-symbol --file ./heap-*.prof --service runtime-pool

B) How to rollback a model-serving config (canary)
1) Check rollout status: ./deployctl status --service=inference-service --env=prod
2) If canary failing, rollback to previous stable: ./deployctl rollback --service=inference-service --rev=previous
3) Observe metrics for 15 minutes on platform/inference/rollouts dashboard before declaring success

5) Retrospective (Q1 2028) — summary and action items
Summary:
- Incident: 2028-02-14 — cross-region routing misconfiguration led to 37 minutes of elevated p99 latency for the API. Root cause: a CI job accidentally replaced traffic-router policy with a default 100% us-east-1 split during a config migration.
- Impact: ~10k failed/slo-violating requests; customer-facing errors for three enterprise customers.
- Detection: Alert api-router-latency-p99 fired after 2 minutes; oncall took 6 minutes to verify; mitigation (traffic split rollback) completed at +37 minutes.
Action items (status):
- Add gating to traffic-router CI job (PR checks) — DONE (2028-03-01)
- Add audit log and automated drift detection for traffic-router policies — IN_PROGRESS (owner: Platform Infra)
- Reduce manual edits to traffic routing in prod; require 2 approvers for changes — DONE (policy enforced)
- Improve runbook steps to include immediate rollback command snippets — DONE (this page updated)

6) Roadmap (Q2 2028)
Goals for the quarter (high-level):
- Reduce runtime cold-start tail by 30% via kernel prewarm and cache priming
- Roll out agentless metric ingestion to reduce metric lag spikes
- Migrate platform dashboards to new Grafana workspace and standardize templating

Planned deliverables and owners:
- Kernel prewarm prototype (MVP) — owner: eng-serving-runtime (Lena) — target: 2028-05-15 — acceptance: p99 cold-start < 1200ms on standard model profile
- Agentless metrics pilot — owner: eng-sre (Olivia) — target: 2028-06-01 — acceptance: metric lag median < 12s across ingestion
- Dashboard migration & templates — owner: eng-platform (Aisha) — target: 2028-05-31 — acceptance: all platform dashboards use common vars and exportable JSON
- Oncall compaction & playbook refresh — owner: eng-platform (Miguel) — target: 2028-04-30 — acceptance: runbook coverage 95% of P1 alerts

Dependencies and risks:
- Cloud quota approvals for additional burst GPU capacity (risk: approval times > 7 days). Mitigation: pre-approved buffer in dedicated pool for Q2 launches.
- Backwards-incompatible telemetry schema changes from metrics-collector (risk: dashboard gaps). Mitigation: staged rollout with feature flags.

- Description: Reason, expected start/end, region, cost center, and owner
- Approver: cloud-ops@redwood.ai
